pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; Types of Weather (CONCEPTUAL, foundational naming — top-centrality node of the domain, 0.13): identify and describe sunny, rainy, windy, snowy, cloudy, foggy, stormy weather and say what today's weather is like using simple vocabulary.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Year 1 'Seasonal changes' (statutory): 'observe and describe weather associated with the seasons'. Weather IS a KS1 science topic in England (unlike the tectonic content, which sits in Geography). State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS, ANCHOR): K-ESS2-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]' (VERIFIED verbatim) — clarification: qualitative observations such as sunny, cloudy, rainy, warm; DCI ESS2.D '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1].' This topic supplies the vocabulary the K-ESS2-1 observation work is built from.
• Operational details — This is the vocabulary bedrock the whole domain builds on (its dependents: Weather vs Climate, Geography & Local Weather, Using Weather Instruments, Seasons, Storm Safety, Rain & Puddles). Keep it concrete and observational: name the weather you can SEE and FEEL out of the window today, match it to a picture/symbol, and build a simple shared weather vocabulary. Anchor to first-hand observation (look outside, a class weather chart) rather than abstractions. No mechanism yet — that comes later (What Causes Wind, The Water Cycle). Evidence targets: name ≥5 weather types; describe today accurately; match weather to symbols.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/observational): the child NAMES at least five weather types, DESCRIBES today's weather accurately in words, and MATCHES weather types to their picture-symbols — grounded in what they can observe, not explained by cause.
bestPractices: Anchor every weather word to first-hand observation — look out of the window and name today's weather — so vocabulary attaches to lived, sensory experience, not just pictures.

Pair each weather type with a canonical simple symbol (sun, cloud, raincloud, snowflake, wind lines) and practise matching both ways, since symbol-reading is an explicit evidence target and a gateway to weather charts.
Build a shared daily weather-chart routine so the same words recur over days and children begin to notice change and repetition (seeding the later patterns-over-time idea).
Engage multiple senses: weather is felt (warm sun, cold wind, wet rain) as well as seen — use sound and touch descriptions to enrich the vocabulary.
Accept and extend everyday words ('freezing', 'boiling', 'chucking it down') toward the shared science vocabulary rather than correcting them away.
Keep it description-only at this age — resist explaining WHY (what causes wind/rain); the naming and noticing is the whole job here.
keyRepresentations: A single illustrated weather scene with each weather type shown and tappable/label-able — the canonical naming surface.
Weather-symbol cards (sun, cloud, rain, snow, wind, fog, storm) matched to photos of real conditions.
A daily class weather chart/calendar where today's weather is marked with a symbol.
Sensory pairing: an image plus a felt-word (sunny–warm, snowy–cold, rainy–wet, windy–blowy).
commonMisconceptions: 'It's a bad/good day' instead of a weather description — children conflate weather with mood/value; steer toward neutral descriptive words.
Cloudy vs foggy vs stormy blur together — distinguish by concrete cues (fog is low and you can't see far; storm has wind + rain + maybe thunder).
'Windy' is judged only by extreme gusts — gentle breezes count too; wind is a spectrum, not just gales.
Weather is only what's overhead now — children may miss that it changes through the day; the daily chart helps them notice.
Snow/ice only 'counts' as weather in storybook winters — include the full local range, and that some places rarely see snow at all.

learn.summary: Foundational weather-naming topic for ages 5–7: children name and describe sunny, rainy, windy, snowy, cloudy, foggy and stormy weather, say what today's weather is like in simple words, and match weather types to symbols. Keep it concrete and observational — name the weather you can see and feel out of the window (looking at the sky and ground, never straight at the sun) — with no mechanism yet (that comes later). The core activity is a tap-to-reveal weather scene that attaches words and symbols to observable cues; strong follow-ons include a weather-report/tally builder (seeding patterns-over-time), matching/describe quizzes for checking vocabulary, and an optional weather-presenter conversation to elicit a child's own words.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal weather scene: name it and say how you can tell
feedback: When a child taps the sun, confirm 'sunny — the sun is shining and you can see shadows' so the word, symbol and observable cue arrive together; if they add 'warm', note that sunny days can be warm or cold.

If a child blurs cloudy, foggy and stormy, use the 'how do you know?' flaps: fog is cloud down low at the ground, so you can't see far; a storm has strong wind with rain (or snow) and maybe thunder and lightning; cloudy means lots of cloud covers the sky (it can be white or grey) but you can still see far.
Accept everyday words like 'freezing', 'boiling' or 'chucking it down' and extend them toward the shared science words rather than correcting them away.
When the child marks today's weather, prompt 'how can you tell?' and praise naming a cue they can actually see or feel — and remind them to look at the sky and ground, never directly at the sun.
activities.rationale: This is a pure naming/vocabulary-and-observation topic; a pre-authored tappable scene reliably ties each word to a symbol and an observable cue, and covers the 5+ types and match-to-symbol targets. Anchoring words to first-hand looking-out-of-the-window observation attaches vocabulary to lived sensory experience, which the NGSS K-ESS2-1 observation work builds from. The 'how can you tell?' flaps teach the concrete cues that separate cloudy, foggy and stormy.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1].' Clarification: qualitative observations such as sunny, cloudy, rainy, warm. DCI ESS2.D: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1].'
learnerActions: Look at one big, inviting weather picture (or a small set of them) showing several weather types at once.

Tap the blazing sun to reveal the word 'sunny', its symbol, and a lift-the-flap 'how can you tell?' that explains 'the sun is shining, the sky is bright and you can see shadows' (a sunny day can still feel cold).

Tap the falling rain to reveal 'rainy'; tap the trees bent sideways and the kite straining on its string to reveal 'windy'; tap the low white blanket you can't see through to reveal 'foggy'; tap the falling snowflakes to reveal 'snowy', the sky full of cloud to reveal 'cloudy', and the dark clouds with lightning and lashing rain to reveal 'stormy'.
For each revealed word, read the symbol shown in the activity's key alongside it (for example sun, cloud, raincloud, snowflake, wind lines, fog, storm) and say the word aloud.

In a 'what's it like today?' corner that mirrors a real class weather chart, look out of the window — at the sky and ground, never straight at the sun — then choose and place the symbol for today's actual weather.
activities.intendedInsight: Each weather type has a name, a symbol, and observable cues you can see or feel — and today's weather can be read directly from the sky and air.

activities.title: Sensory pairing: weather you feel as well as see
feedback: Encourage both a seen cue and a felt cue for each weather word (e.g. sunny: 'the sun is shining and there are shadows' and 'I can feel the sun on my skin', even if the air is cold).
If a child only describes the picture, prompt 'what would it feel like outside?' to bring in touch and sound.
activities.rationale: Engaging multiple senses attaches weather vocabulary to richer lived experience, and keeps the focus descriptive rather than explanatory at this age.
learnerActions: Look at each weather image and pair it with a sense-word: sunny–bright (you may feel the sun on your skin, even on a cold day), snowy–cold, rainy–wet, windy–blowy.
Describe both what you can see and what it would feel like on your skin for today's weather.
Use sound and touch descriptions (the whoosh of wind, the patter of rain) to add to the weather word.
activities.intendedInsight: Weather is experienced through more than one sense — it is felt and heard as well as seen — which enriches the descriptive vocabulary.

activities.title: Build today's weather report and tally the week
feedback: Praise using the same shared weather words across days so children hear them recur.

If a child thinks today's weather is fixed, recall a day that changed from morning to afternoon from your own observation — the weather can change through the day as well as from day to day. (A once-per-day chart only shows change across days, so within-day change comes from looking out, not from the chart.)
activities.rationale: A build/tally surface seeds the patterns-over-time idea named in K-ESS2-1 and makes the daily weather-chart routine concrete. The weekly chart records change and repetition across days; within-day change is noticed through first-hand observation, since a once-per-day chart does not itself capture morning-to-afternoon change. It is a follow-on to naming, not the first exposure: at this age the core job is naming and recognising, so keep interactions to simple drag-and-place.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1].' Clarification: qualitative observations such as sunny, cloudy, rainy, warm. DCI ESS2.D: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1].'
learnerActions: Drag weather symbols onto a simple map or report to 'build today's weather report'.
Over a week, add a symbol each day to a tally chart and count how many sunny, rainy or cloudy days there were.

Talk about which weather happened most across the week, and from looking out of the window recall that the weather can also change within a single day (e.g. sunny in the morning, rainy by the afternoon).
activities.intendedInsight: Weather recurs and changes over days — recording it with the same words and symbols lets you notice patterns over time — and it can also change within a single day.

activities.title: Match and describe: check the vocabulary
feedback: For a correct match, restate the cue that justified it ('yes — grey cloud all over, so cloudy').
For the grey-sky scene, if a child says 'no weather', widen the category: cloudy, windy and foggy are all weather; ask what the sky and air are doing, not just what is falling.
activities.rationale: The match-weather-to-symbol evidence target is literally a matching task, and a describe-the-scene choice cleanly checks vocabulary. This verifies the naming rather than building it, so use it to confirm after the exploratory scene; matching alone does not elicit the child's own spoken or built description.
learnerActions: Match each photo of real weather to the correct word and its symbol, going both ways (photo→word and symbol→word).
Choose which word best describes a shown scene (e.g. a grey overcast sky with nothing falling → 'cloudy').
Say what today's weather is in a full short sentence using the shared words.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm that the weather words and symbols have stuck and can be applied to real conditions.

activities.title: Weather-reporter chat: say what it's like out there (optional)
feedback: Gently extend a child's everyday word toward the shared science word (e.g. 'chucking it down' → 'rainy, really heavy rain').
If a child names only the temperature, ask separately what the sky is doing to pull weather and temperature apart.
activities.rationale: Eliciting spoken description gives production practice beyond recognition and is pleasant and age-appropriate. A naming task does not require open dialogue, so this is an optional complement where a child benefits from speaking their own words.
learnerActions: Pretend to be a weather reporter and tell a friendly presenter what the weather is like today.
Answer 'how can you tell?' by naming a cue you can see or feel.
Extend your own words when the presenter offers the matching shared weather word.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can produce weather descriptions in their own words, not just recognise them.

constraints: Keep it description-only at this age: name and notice the weather; do not explain WHY (what causes wind or rain) — mechanism belongs to later topics.
Steer away from value/mood judgements ('a bad/good day') toward neutral descriptive words.
Treat wind as a spectrum — gentle breezes count, not only gales — and include the full local weather range, noting some places rarely see snow.
Picture/scene work is a scaffold: pair it with real looking-out-of-the-window observation and a daily class weather chart so vocabulary attaches to lived experience, not just images.
Separate weather from temperature: you can have cold sunny days and warm cloudy days.
Matching and multiple-choice items verify vocabulary but do not elicit the child's own spoken or built description; use a production or build activity for that.
The weather report/tally builder is a follow-on; keep interactions to simple drag-and-place for ages 5–7.
A once-per-day tally chart records change across days; within-day change is noticed through direct observation, not read off the chart.
Safety: when observing sunny weather, look at the sky and the ground — never look directly at the sun.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The DfE KS1 'Seasonal changes' source is marked verified:false in the row (verbatim from a prior-session fetch, not re-fetched); treat the UK standards claim as unverified.

The source row rated a 3D environment as 'poor' for this topic; that is a fit judgement about added cost/distraction for a naming task, not established evidence that 3D adds nothing pedagogically. It is not asserted here as a universal law.

Original diagnostic uses an overcast grey sky with nothing falling as the discriminating item for 'cloudy' vs 'no weather'; retained as pedagogically sound, with 'no weather' handled only as a misconception to correct, never offered as a valid answer.
Added a sun-safety reminder for the looking-out-of-the-window observation, as the activities direct young children to observe sunny weather first-hand.

probeDeeper: Name me five different kinds of weather.
If those grey clouds start dropping tiny water, what type of weather is it then?
Is it sunny today AND could it also be cold? How can both be true?
assess.correctAnswer: It's cloudy (overcast). You can tell by looking at the sky — it's covered in grey clouds — even though nothing is falling and the sun isn't showing. Cloudy is a type of weather, just like sunny or rainy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Weather = only rain or sun — 'if nothing is falling there's no weather'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Widen the category: cloudy, windy, foggy are all weather too; ask what the sky and air are doing, not just what's falling.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's no weather right now because it isn't raining and the sun isn't out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says there is no weather right now because it isn't raining and the sun isn't out

errorPatterns.pattern: Sun means hot / weather equals temperature — 'if the sun is out it's always hot'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two: you can have cold sunny days and warm cloudy days; the weather is what the sky and air are doing, temperature is how warm it is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates a sunny sky with being hot regardless of the actual air, or describes only temperature when asked about weather

responseLevels.gap: Says there's 'no weather' when nothing is falling, or names only rain and sun as weather.
responseLevels.full: Names five or more weather types, reads the current weather from the sky (cloudy) even with nothing falling, matches types to symbols, and separates weather from temperature.
responseLevels.partial: Names several weather types and reads today's from the sky, but leans on what's falling and misses cloudy/windy/foggy as weather in their own right.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look outside (or at this picture): the sky is grey and full of clouds, but no rain is falling and the sun isn't out. Tell me what the weather is like right now, and how you can tell.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the full range of weather types names 'cloudy' from the sky alone. A child who thinks weather means only rain or sun says 'there's no weather' because nothing is falling — the tell.
